name: Map ≠ territory
rule: Every model leaves things out, so know where yours breaks.
plain: A map is useful because it simplifies. Know which simplifications matter here.

story.beat: The colony's oxygen simulator, built on Earth, says the greenhouse should be fine. Ada pulls it apart: it models plants and lamps but not soil microbes, which also breathe oxygen. The map left out a living part of the territory. The comms tower plays an archive transmission: Biosphere 2.

examples.text: The solar model assumes clear skies. Dust storms aren't on that map, so the storage plan must allow for them.
The rock model treats the crust as uniform. The drill hits a hidden void the map never showed.
The price model assumes rational traders. During the panic, nobody behaves like the map.

sim.try: Add the two missing factors to the model and watch it catch up with reality.

realCase.title: Biosphere 2's vanishing oxygen
realCase.text: Eight people sealed themselves inside a 1.27-hectare artificial world in Arizona. Over 16 months, oxygen fell from 20.9% to about 14.5%, and fresh oxygen had to be pumped in. The designers' model had missed two things: rich soil full of microbes consuming oxygen, and fresh concrete absorbing the CO2 that should have been recycled back into oxygen.
realCase.source: Severinghaus et al., 'Oxygen loss in Biosphere 2', Eos (1994)

misuse: Rejecting all models because none are perfect. The question isn't 'is it true?' but 'is it useful here, and where does it break?'

predict.prompt: The Earth-built simulator says oxygen should be fine, but it isn't. Most likely reason?
options: The model leaves out something that matters here
predict.why: When a model and reality disagree, look for what the map omits.

options: Soil microbes plus concrete absorbing CO2
mcq.why: Both were missing from the design model.

whichModel.prompt: Newton's laws predict a satellite clock perfectly, except that GPS needs relativity corrections or errors of about 10 km build up each day.
whichModel.why: A great model applied past its limits.
